AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To investigate the impacts of the Farm to School (FTS) program on the selection and consumption of fruits and vegetables.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: Plate waste data were recorded using the visual inspection method before and after implementation of the program.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Six elementary schools in Florida: 3 treatment and 3 control schools.

AbstractText.Label: PARTICIPANTS
AbstractText.content: A total of 11,262 meal observations of National School Lunch Program (NSLP) participants in grades 1-5.

AbstractText.Label: INTERVENTION
AbstractText.content: The FTS program, specifically local procurement of NSLP offerings, began in treatment schools in November, 2015 after the researchers collected preintervention data.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
AbstractText.content: The NSLP participants' selection and consumption of fruits and vegetables.

AbstractText.Label: ANALYSIS
AbstractText.content: Data were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U and proportions tests and difference-in-difference regressions.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: The NSLP participants at the treatment schools consumed, on average, 0.061 (P = .002) more servings of vegetables and 0.055 (P = .05) more servings of fruit after implementation of the FTS program. When school-level fixed effects are included, ordinary least squares and tobit regression results indicated that NSLP participants at the treatment schools respectively consumed 0.107 (P < .001) and 0.086 (P < .001) more servings of vegetables, on average, after implementation of the FTS program.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS
AbstractText.content: Local procurement positively affected healthy eating.
